claim: Glioblastoma (GBM) harbors a highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) which influences glioma growth.
source: Glioblastoma (GBM) harbors a highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) which influences glioma growth.
evidence: This is a general statement about GBM characteristics that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: The study performed high-depth single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) on paired biopsies from the tumor center, peripheral infiltration zone and blood of five primary GBM patients.
source: Here, we performed high-depth single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) on paired biopsies from the tumor center, peripheral infiltration zone and blood of five primary GBM patients.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The analysis included more than 45,000 cells.
source: Through analysis of >45,000 cells, we revealed a regionally distinct transcription profile of microglia (MG) and monocyte-derived macrophages (MdMs) and an impaired activation signature in the tumor-peripheral cytotoxic-cell compartment.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Microglia (MG) and monocyte-derived macrophages (MdMs) display regionally distinct transcription profiles.
source: Through analysis of >45,000 cells, we revealed a regionally distinct transcription profile of microglia (MG) and monocyte-derived macrophages (MdMs) and an impaired activation signature in the tumor-peripheral cytotoxic-cell compartment.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The tumor-peripheral cytotoxic-cell compartment exhibits an impaired activation signature.
source: Through analysis of >45,000 cells, we revealed a regionally distinct transcription profile of microglia (MG) and monocyte-derived macrophages (MdMs) and an impaired activation signature in the tumor-peripheral cytotoxic-cell compartment.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: CX3CR1high CD8+ T cells with effector phenotype are enriched in blood but absent in the TME.
source: Comparing tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells with circulating cells identified CX3CR1high and CX3CR1int CD8+ T cells with effector and memory phenotype, respectively, enriched in blood but absent in the TME.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing CD8+ T cells between blood and tumor samples.

claim: CX3CR1int CD8+ T cells with memory phenotype are enriched in blood but absent in the TME.
source: Comparing tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells with circulating cells identified CX3CR1high and CX3CR1int CD8+ T cells with effector and memory phenotype, respectively, enriched in blood but absent in the TME.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing CD8+ T cells between blood and tumor samples.

claim: Tumor CD8+ T cells display a tissue-resident memory phenotype with dysfunctional features.
source: Tumor CD8+ T cells displayed a tissue-resident memory phenotype with dysfunctional features.
evidence: This is a characterization of tumor CD8+ T cells based on gene expression analysis.

claim: The current standard of care for GBM consists of tumor resection followed by adjuvant chemoradiotherapy resulting in a median overall survival of only 14 months.
source: The current standard of care consists of tumor resection followed by adjuvant chemoradiotherapy resulting in a median overall survival of only 14 months (Stupp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stupp et al., 2005.

claim: GBM-induced aberrant vessels nourish glioma cells and provide a specialized niche for tumor-associated stromal and immune cells.
source: The GBM-induced aberrant vessels not only nourish glioma cells, but also provide a specialized niche for tumor-associated stromal and immune cells such as monocyte-derived macrophages (MdMs), yolk sac-derived microglia (MG; together termed glioma-associated macrophages/microglia, GAMs), and peripheral adaptive immune cells.
evidence: This is a statement about GBM biology based on established knowledge.

claim: The immune tumor microenvironment (iTME) acts in an immunosuppressive manner and promotes tumor progression.
source: This immune tumor microenvironment (iTME) paradoxically acts in an immunosuppressive manner and promotes tumor progression (Bowman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bowman et al., 2016.

claim: Clinical trials of systemic T cell checkpoint blockade in GBM showed disappointing results.
source: For example, clinical trials of systemic T cell checkpoint blockade showed only disappointing results (Reardon et al., 2017a; Reardon et al., 2017b), which was attributed in part to the immunosuppressive components of the GBM iTME.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reardon et al., 2017a and 2017b.

claim: The disappointing results of checkpoint blockade trials were attributed in part to the immunosuppressive components of the GBM iTME.
source: For example, clinical trials of systemic T cell checkpoint blockade showed only disappointing results (Reardon et al., 2017a; Reardon et al., 2017b), which was attributed in part to the immunosuppressive components of the GBM iTME.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: Major efforts have been undertaken to describe the GBM iTME on a single-cell level.
source: Hence, major efforts have been undertaken to describe the GBM iTME on a single-cell level (Klemm et al., 2020; Friebel et al., 2020; Abdelfattah et al., 2022), or dissect the composition and changes upon disease stages, recurrence and immunotherapy specifically within the GAM compartment (Pombo Antunes et al., 2021; Goswami et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Human data on the composition of the iTME in different tumor regions remain scarce.
source: However, human data on the composition of the iTME in different tumor regions (contrast enhancing tumor center versus peripheral infiltration zone) remain scarce (Darmanis et al., 2017; Landry et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The tumor center was defined as contrast enhancing by MRI-guided, navigated surgical resection.
source: The tumor center was defined as contrast enhancing, whereas the tumor periphery was defined as T2 hyperintense by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided, navigated surgical resection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the methodology for defining tumor regions.

claim: The tumor periphery was defined as T2 hyperintense by MRI-guided, navigated surgical resection.
source: The tumor center was defined as contrast enhancing, whereas the tumor periphery was defined as T2 hyperintense by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided, navigated surgical resection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the methodology for defining tumor regions.

claim: Increased cellular density of the center vs. periphery samples was confirmed by nuclear DAPI staining.
source: Increased cellular density of the center vs. periphery samples was confirmed by nuclear DAPI staining on matched histological micrographs of the resected tissue specimens used for scRNA-seq (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI staining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A total of 45,466 cells passed initial quality control and filtering.
source: In total, we analyzed 45,466 cells that passed initial quality control and filtering, comprising 8254 cells from tumor center, 5954 cells from tumor periphery and 31,258 PBMCs, with 6354–10,957 cells per patient (Supplementary file 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data processing.

claim: The dataset comprised 8254 cells from tumor center, 5954 cells from tumor periphery and 31,258 PBMCs.
source: In total, we analyzed 45,466 cells that passed initial quality control and filtering, comprising 8254 cells from tumor center, 5954 cells from tumor periphery and 31,258 PBMCs, with 6354–10,957 cells per patient (Supplementary file 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative breakdown of the dataset.

claim: The dataset included 6354–10,957 cells per patient.
source: In total, we analyzed 45,466 cells that passed initial quality control and filtering, comprising 8254 cells from tumor center, 5954 cells from tumor periphery and 31,258 PBMCs, with 6354–10,957 cells per patient (Supplementary file 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the dataset.

claim: A good overlap of cells across patients was observed for most of the dataset.
source: As we observed a good overlap of cells across patients for most of the dataset (see Methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–F), we chose not to perform any correction for patient-specific effects.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, supported by figures.

claim: No correction for patient-specific effects was performed due to good overlap of cells across patients.
source: As we observed a good overlap of cells across patients for most of the dataset (see Methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–F), we chose not to perform any correction for patient-specific effects.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on data characteristics.

claim: Hierarchical clustering partitioned cells into clusters which were annotated into nine distinct cell types for the immune subset.
source: Using hierarchical clustering, the cells were partitioned into clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) which were then annotated into nine distinct cell types for the immune subset, including two transcriptionally distinct MG subsets (MG_1 and MG_2) and four cell types for the CD45-negative subset (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the clustering and annotation methodology and results.

claim: Two transcriptionally distinct MG subsets (MG_1 and MG_2) were identified.
source: Using hierarchical clustering, the cells were partitioned into clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) which were then annotated into nine distinct cell types for the immune subset, including two transcriptionally distinct MG subsets (MG_1 and MG_2) and four cell types for the CD45-negative subset (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: Four cell types were identified for the CD45-negative subset.
source: Using hierarchical clustering, the cells were partitioned into clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) which were then annotated into nine distinct cell types for the immune subset, including two transcriptionally distinct MG subsets (MG_1 and MG_2) and four cell types for the CD45-negative subset (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: The abundance of CD4+ T cell clusters increased in periphery compared to center.
source: Differential abundance analysis between tumor center and periphery did not reveal significant changes, but some populations displayed suggestive differences: the abundance of both CD4+ T cell and monocytic clusters increased in periphery compared to center, while the abundance of MdM clusters decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from differential abundance analysis, though not statistically significant.

claim: The abundance of monocytic clusters increased in periphery compared to center.
source: Differential abundance analysis between tumor center and periphery did not reveal significant changes, but some populations displayed suggestive differences: the abundance of both CD4+ T cell and monocytic clusters increased in periphery compared to center, while the abundance of MdM clusters decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from differential abundance analysis, though not statistically significant.

claim: The abundance of MdM clusters decreased in periphery compared to center.
source: Differential abundance analysis between tumor center and periphery did not reveal significant changes, but some populations displayed suggestive differences: the abundance of both CD4+ T cell and monocytic clusters increased in periphery compared to center, while the abundance of MdM clusters decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from differential abundance analysis, though not statistically significant.

claim: The decreased abundance of MdMs in the tumor periphery has been observed by others.
source: This has been observed by others as well (Darmanis et al., 2017; Pinton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MG_1 subset of MG showed increased abundance in the tumor periphery.
source: Indeed, within the innate immune population (Figure 2E) we confirmed the decreased abundance of MdMs in the tumor periphery and noticed an increased abundance of the MG_1 subset of MG in the tumor periphery. (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from the miloR differential abundance analysis.

claim: Peripheral MG showed downregulation of inflammatory-related genes FCGBP and CCL20.
source: Differential expression analysis between MG from tumor center and periphery revealed downregulation of inflammatory-related genes in the peripheral MG (FCGBP and CCL20), downregulation of genes associated with canonical interferon (IFN) responses (IFI6, IFI27, STAT1, ISG15), and cell proliferation (STMN1) as well as downregulation of scavenger receptor gene CD163 (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral MG showed downregulation of genes associated with canonical interferon (IFN) responses (IFI6, IFI27, STAT1, ISG15).
source: Differential expression analysis between MG from tumor center and periphery revealed downregulation of inflammatory-related genes in the peripheral MG (FCGBP and CCL20), downregulation of genes associated with canonical interferon (IFN) responses (IFI6, IFI27, STAT1, ISG15), and cell proliferation (STMN1) as well as downregulation of scavenger receptor gene CD163 (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral MG showed downregulation of cell proliferation gene STMN1.
source: Differential expression analysis between MG from tumor center and periphery revealed downregulation of inflammatory-related genes in the peripheral MG (FCGBP and CCL20), downregulation of genes associated with canonical interferon (IFN) responses (IFI6, IFI27, STAT1, ISG15), and cell proliferation (STMN1) as well as downregulation of scavenger receptor gene CD163 (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral MG showed downregulation of scavenger receptor gene CD163.
source: Differential expression analysis between MG from tumor center and periphery revealed downregulation of inflammatory-related genes in the peripheral MG (FCGBP and CCL20), downregulation of genes associated with canonical interferon (IFN) responses (IFI6, IFI27, STAT1, ISG15), and cell proliferation (STMN1) as well as downregulation of scavenger receptor gene CD163 (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: CD163 was shown to have a potential role in the phagocytic response of MG to beta-amyloid depositions in postmortem human brain.
source: The latter was shown to have a potential role in the phagocytic response of MG to beta-amyloid depositions identified in single-nucleus RNA-seq of postmortem human brain (Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2020.

claim: ID1 was found to be increased in the peripheral MG.
source: Among many upregulated genes whose function is not yet known, we found Inhibitor of DNA-Binding 1, also known as Inhibitor of Differentiation 1 (ID1) to be increased in the peripheral MG (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: ID1 is well described in GBM progression, treatment resistance and glioma stem cell biology.
source: ID1 is well described in GBM progression, treatment resistance and glioma stem cell biology (Soroceanu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Soroceanu et al., 2013.

claim: ID1 has been linked to suppression of the anti-tumor immune response in the myeloid compartment and promoting tumor progression.
source: However, new evidence has emerged, linking ID1 to suppression of the anti-tumor immune response in the myeloid compartment and promoting tumor progression (Papaspyridonos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Papaspyridonos et al., 2015.

claim: GSEA revealed significant downregulation of GO categories involved in antigen processing and presentation via MHC-I and MHC-II in the peripheral MG relative to the center MG.
source: To further explore the underlying biological processes differing between MG in the two compartments, we conducted a gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on the results of the differential expression analysis using Gene Ontology (GO) database (Biological Processes). This revealed overall a significant downregulation of GO categories involved in antigen processing and presentation via MHC-I and MHC-II in the peripheral MG relative to the center MG, as well as downregulation of amino acid metabolism and TNF-α signaling pathway (Figure 3B), which supported the conclusion of an impaired activation state of peripheral MG.
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA analysis.

claim: GSEA revealed downregulation of amino acid metabolism in the peripheral MG relative to the center MG.
source: This revealed overall a significant downregulation of GO categories involved in antigen processing and presentation via MHC-I and MHC-II in the peripheral MG relative to the center MG, as well as downregulation of amino acid metabolism and TNF-α signaling pathway (Figure 3B), which supported the conclusion of an impaired activation state of peripheral MG.
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA analysis.

claim: GSEA revealed downregulation of TNF-α signaling pathway in the peripheral MG relative to the center MG.
source: This revealed overall a significant downregulation of GO categories involved in antigen processing and presentation via MHC-I and MHC-II in the peripheral MG relative to the center MG, as well as downregulation of amino acid metabolism and TNF-α signaling pathway (Figure 3B), which supported the conclusion of an impaired activation state of peripheral MG.
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA analysis.

claim: DCs showed upregulation of pro-inflammatory related gene sets in the tumor periphery compared to tumor center.
source: When comparing the transcriptional profiles of the other innate immune phagocytic populations, DCs and MdMs, we observed for both cell types upregulation of pro-inflammatory related gene sets in the tumor periphery compared to tumor center (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression and GSEA analysis.

claim: MdMs showed upregulation of pro-inflammatory related gene sets in the tumor periphery compared to tumor center.
source: When comparing the transcriptional profiles of the other innate immune phagocytic populations, DCs and MdMs, we observed for both cell types upregulation of pro-inflammatory related gene sets in the tumor periphery compared to tumor center (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression and GSEA analysis.

claim: The induced pro-inflammatory phenotype in DCs was also observed when comparing DCs from tumor periphery to PBMC-derived ones.
source: Within DCs, the induced pro-inflammatory phenotype was also observed when comparing DCs from tumor periphery to PBMC-derived ones (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: DCs and MdMs have a proinflammatory phenotype in the glioma periphery as opposed to MG.
source: Taken together, DCs and MdMs seem to have a proinflammatory phenotype in the glioma periphery as opposed to MG.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the differential expression analyses.

claim: MdMs are less abundant in the glioma periphery compared to the tumor center.
source: However, they are less abundant there, at least as far as MdMs are concerned (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from differential abundance analysis.

claim: The MG_1 cluster was highly enriched for the activator protein-1 (AP-1) family of transcription factors including FOS, FOSB, JUN, JUNB, MAF, and MAFB.
source: The MG_1 cluster was highly enriched for the activator protein-1 (AP-1) family of transcription factors including FOS, FOSB, JUN, JUNB, MAF, and MAFB (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 5), which convey a surveilling phenotype to adult MG, but are also involved in numerous processes including cell growth, differentiation, and immune activation (Holtman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from cluster-specific gene analysis.

claim: AP-1 transcription factors convey a surveilling phenotype to adult MG and are involved in cell growth, differentiation, and immune activation.
source: The MG_1 cluster was highly enriched for the activator protein-1 (AP-1) family of transcription factors including FOS, FOSB, JUN, JUNB, MAF, and MAFB (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 5), which convey a surveilling phenotype to adult MG, but are also involved in numerous processes including cell growth, differentiation, and immune activation (Holtman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holtman et al., 2017.

claim: FOSB gene products were implicated in the excitotoxic MG activation by regulating complement C5a receptor expression.
source: Specifically, FOSB gene products were implicated in the excitotoxic MG activation by regulating complement C5a receptor expression (Nomaru et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nomaru et al., 2014.

claim: MG_1 cells showed concomitant upregulation of anti-inflammatory Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2).
source: Yet, concomitant upregulation of anti-inflammatory Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) (Sweet et al., 2020) and Dual Specificity Protein Phosphatase 1 (DUSP1), an inhibitor of innate inflammation by negatively regulating the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (Salojin et al., 2006), together with increased expression of anti-proliferative genes like RHOB, BTG1 and BTG2 paint a more complex picture of these cells.
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, with citation support for KLF2 function.

claim: KLF2 is anti-inflammatory.
source: Yet, concomitant upregulation of anti-inflammatory Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) (Sweet et al., 2020) and Dual Specificity Protein Phosphatase 1 (DUSP1), an inhibitor of innate inflammation by negatively regulating the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (Salojin et al., 2006), together with increased expression of anti-proliferative genes like RHOB, BTG1 and BTG2 paint a more complex picture of these cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sweet et al., 2020.

claim: DUSP1 is an inhibitor of innate inflammation by negatively regulating the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.
source: Yet, concomitant upregulation of anti-inflammatory Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) (Sweet et al., 2020) and Dual Specificity Protein Phosphatase 1 (DUSP1), an inhibitor of innate inflammation by negatively regulating the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (Salojin et al., 2006), together with increased expression of anti-proliferative genes like RHOB, BTG1 and BTG2 paint a more complex picture of these cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Salojin et al., 2006.

claim: MG_1 cells showed increased expression of anti-proliferative genes like RHOB, BTG1 and BTG2.
source: Yet, concomitant upregulation of anti-inflammatory Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) (Sweet et al., 2020) and Dual Specificity Protein Phosphatase 1 (DUSP1), an inhibitor of innate inflammation by negatively regulating the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (Salojin et al., 2006), together with increased expression of anti-proliferative genes like RHOB, BTG1 and BTG2 paint a more complex picture of these cells.
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis.

claim: BTG1 was identified as an activation-induced apoptotic sensitizer in MG after exposure to inflammatory stimuli.
source: Particularly, BTG1 was identified as an activation-induced apoptotic sensitizer in MG after exposure to inflammatory stimuli (Lee et al., 2003), serving as an autoregulatory mechanism and possibly hinting towards an exhausted state in these MG_1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2003.

claim: BTG1 serves as an autoregulatory mechanism and possibly hints towards an exhausted state in MG_1 cells.
source: Particularly, BTG1 was identified as an activation-induced apoptotic sensitizer in MG after exposure to inflammatory stimuli (Lee et al., 2003), serving as an autoregulatory mechanism and possibly hinting towards an exhausted state in these MG_1 cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature and observed gene expression.

claim: GSEA revealed downregulation of many MG effector functions in the MG_1 population including inflammation, immune cell activation, and immunometabolism.
source: GSEA for differences between MG_1 and MG_2 clusters using the MSigDB Hallmark collection of major biological pathways (Liberzon et al., 2015) revealed downregulation of many MG effector functions in the MG_1 population including (1) inflammation ('Complement', 'Allograft Rejection', 'Reactive Oxygen Species Pathway'), (2) immune cell activation ('IFN-α Response', 'IFN-γ Response', 'IL6 JAK STAT3 Signaling'), and (3) immunometabolism ('Fatty Acid Metabolism', 'Oxidative Phosphorylation', 'Glycolysis'; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA analysis.

claim: MG_1 cluster showed reduced expression of reactivity markers C1QA, FCGR1A, CD14, HLA-DRA, TREM2, and Ferritin (FTH1) compared to MG_2 cells.
source: As we examined the expression of previously described reactivity markers of MG including C1QA, FCGR1A, CD14, HLA-DRA, TREM2, and Ferritin (FTH1) (Walker and Lue, 2015; Hopperton et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2019; McQuade et al., 2020; Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), and established MG homeostatic genes like CX3CR1, HEXB and SPI1 (PU.1) (Supplementary file 5), we noted a reduced expression of these genes in the MG_1 cluster compared to MG_2 cells, while the anti-inflammatory transcription factors NR4A1 (Rothe et al., 2017) NR4A2 (Saijo et al., 2009) were highly upregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, with citations supporting the characterization of these markers.

claim: MG_1 cluster showed reduced expression of homeostatic genes CX3CR1, HEXB and SPI1 (PU.1) compared to MG_2 cells.
source: As we examined the expression of previously described reactivity markers of MG including C1QA, FCGR1A, CD14, HLA-DRA, TREM2, and Ferritin (FTH1) (Walker and Lue, 2015; Hopperton et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2019; McQuade et al., 2020; Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), and established MG homeostatic genes like CX3CR1, HEXB and SPI1 (PU.1) (Supplementary file 5), we noted a reduced expression of these genes in the MG_1 cluster compared to MG_2 cells, while the anti-inflammatory transcription factors NR4A1 (Rothe et al., 2017) NR4A2 (Saijo et al., 2009) were highly upregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis.

claim: Anti-inflammatory transcription factors NR4A1 and NR4A2 were highly upregulated in MG_1 cluster.
source: As we examined the expression of previously described reactivity markers of MG including C1QA, FCGR1A, CD14, HLA-DRA, TREM2, and Ferritin (FTH1) (Walker and Lue, 2015; Hopperton et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2019; McQuade et al., 2020; Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), and established MG homeostatic genes like CX3CR1, HEXB and SPI1 (PU.1) (Supplementary file 5), we noted a reduced expression of these genes in the MG_1 cluster compared to MG_2 cells, while the anti-inflammatory transcription factors NR4A1 (Rothe et al., 2017) NR4A2 (Saijo et al., 2009) were highly upregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, with citations supporting the anti-inflammatory function.

claim: MG_1 cells showed increased abundance in the tumor periphery among total MG.
source: Additionally, when comparing the distribution of MG subsets between sites among total MG, we observed an increased abundance of MG_1 cells in the tumor periphery, which might at least partially explain the previously observed impaired activation state of total peripheral MG (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from differential abundance analysis.

claim: The non-reactive phenotype is a common feature for all peripheral MG and is not only driven by a differential abundance pattern of one MG subpopulation relative to the other.
source: To rule out this explanation, we stratified the differential expression analysis between tumor periphery and center by MG subtype and observed similar genes downregulated in the tumor periphery in each subtype (e.g. CCL20, FCGBP; Supplementary file 5), arguing that the non-reactive phenotype is a common feature for all peripheral MG and is not only driven by a differential abundance pattern of one MG subpopulation relative to the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on stratified differential expression analysis.

claim: Very few significant changes were observed in the transcriptomic profiles of CD4+ T cells between tumor center and periphery.
source: Next, we investigated the regional differences in the lymphoid compartment composed of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. We observed only very few significant changes in the transcriptomic profiles of CD4+ T cells between tumor center and periphery (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Comparing peripheral CD8+ T cells with CD8+ T cells from tumor center revealed 110 differentially expressed genes (43 genes upregulated and 67 genes downregulated).
source: Yet, comparing peripheral CD8+ T cells with CD8+ T cells from tumor center revealed 110 differentially expressed genes (43 genes upregulated and 67 genes downregulated; Figure 4A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from differential expression analysis.

claim: Many downregulated genes in the peripheral CD8+ T cells associated with canonical IFN responses (IFI6, IFI27, MX1, STAT1, EPSTI1 PARP9, ISG15).
source: Many downregulated genes in the peripheral CD8+ T cells associated with canonical IFN responses (IFI6, IFI27, MX1, STAT1, EPSTI1 PARP9, ISG15; Szabo et al., 2019), cell proliferation (STMN1, CENPF, HELLS, NUSAP1, and DNPH1) and T cell co-stimulation (CD28, TMIGD2 [CD28H], TNFRSF4 [OX40], CD27 and TNFRSF18 [GITR]; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis, with citation support for IFN response genes.

claim: Many downregulated genes in the peripheral CD8+ T cells associated with cell proliferation (STMN1, CENPF, HELLS, NUSAP1, and DNPH1).
source: Many downregulated genes in the peripheral CD8+ T cells associated with canonical IFN responses (IFI6, IFI27, MX1, STAT1, EPSTI1 PARP9, ISG15; Szabo et al., 2019), cell proliferation (STMN1, CENPF, HELLS, NUSAP1, and DNPH1) and T cell co-stimulation (CD28, TMIGD2 [CD28H], TNFRSF4 [OX40], CD27 and TNFRSF18 [GITR]; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Many downregulated genes in the peripheral CD8+ T cells associated with T cell co-stimulation (CD28, TMIGD2 [CD28H], TNFRSF4 [OX40], CD27 and TNFRSF18 [GITR]).
source: Many downregulated genes in the peripheral CD8+ T cells associated with canonical IFN responses (IFI6, IFI27, MX1, STAT1, EPSTI1 PARP9, ISG15; Szabo et al., 2019), cell proliferation (STMN1, CENPF, HELLS, NUSAP1, and DNPH1) and T cell co-stimulation (CD28, TMIGD2 [CD28H], TNFRSF4 [OX40], CD27 and TNFRSF18 [GITR]; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: CTLA4 was upregulated in the center CD8+ T cells.
source: Contrary to our expectations, we saw upregulation of CTLA4 in the center CD8+ T cells which acts as a negative costimulatory molecule.
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: CTLA-4 is not constitutively expressed on T lymphocytes but only induced following T cell activation.
source: However, unlike other costimulatory receptors, such as CD27 and CD28, CTLA-4 is not constitutively expressed on T lymphocytes (Alegre et al., 1996). but only induced following T cell activation, along with positive costimulatory molecules such as OX40 and GITR.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alegre et al., 1996.

claim: Upregulation of CTLA-4 requires entry into the cell cycle.
source: In addition, upregulation of CTLA-4 requires entry into the cell cycle (Alegre et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alegre et al., 1996.

claim: CTLA-4 induction in center CD8+ T cells suggested T cell activation rather than exhaustion.
source: In summary, CTLA-4 induction in center CD8+ T cells rather suggested T cell activation than exhaustion, especially since other inhibitory receptors like PDCD1 (PD-1), LAG3 and HAVCR2 (TIM-3) were not differentially expressed between sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on gene expression patterns and biological knowledge.

claim: Inhibitory receptors PDCD1 (PD-1), LAG3 and HAVCR2 (TIM-3) were not differentially expressed between sites in CD8+ T cells.
source: In summary, CTLA-4 induction in center CD8+ T cells rather suggested T cell activation than exhaustion, especially since other inhibitory receptors like PDCD1 (PD-1), LAG3 and HAVCR2 (TIM-3) were not differentially expressed between sites.
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: No differential expression of genes involved in CD8+ T cell effector functions like cytotoxicity (e.g. GZMK, GZMB, KLRG1, PRF1) or cytokines (e.g. CCL5, XCL1, XCL2, IL10) was observed between sites.
source: Moreover, we did not observe differential expression of genes involved in CD8+ T cell effector functions like cytotoxicity (e.g. GZMK, GZMB, KLRG1, PRF1) or cytokines (e.g. CCL5, XCL1, XCL2, IL10).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral CD8+ T cells showed upregulation of inhibitory genes TGFB1 and FCRL6.
source: Yet, we noted upregulation of inhibitory genes (TGFB1 and FCRL6 Johnson et al., 2018) in the peripheral CD8+ T cells, suggesting that a pool of activated, proliferating and IFN-responsive CD8+ T cells is present in the tumor center, however, absent in the tumor periphery.
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis, with citation support for FCRL6.

claim: A pool of activated, proliferating and IFN-responsive CD8+ T cells is present in the tumor center but absent in the tumor periphery.
source: Yet, we noted upregulation of inhibitory genes (TGFB1 and FCRL6 Johnson et al., 2018) in the peripheral CD8+ T cells, suggesting that a pool of activated, proliferating and IFN-responsive CD8+ T cells is present in the tumor center, however, absent in the tumor periphery.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential expression patterns observed.

claim: Peripheral NK cells showed reduced IFN response (MX1 and IFI44L).
source: Similar trends were observed for the peripheral NK cell population with peripherally reduced IFN response (MX1 and IFI44L), and proliferative genes (STMN1, HELLS, CENPF, PTTG1, and DNPH1), downregulated stimulatory receptors (TMIGD2 [CD28H] and TNFRSF18 [GITR]), and reduced NF-κB signaling (NFKB1 and RELB; Figure 4B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral NK cells showed reduced proliferative genes (STMN1, HELLS, CENPF, PTTG1, and DNPH1).
source: Similar trends were observed for the peripheral NK cell population with peripherally reduced IFN response (MX1 and IFI44L), and proliferative genes (STMN1, HELLS, CENPF, PTTG1, and DNPH1), downregulated stimulatory receptors (TMIGD2 [CD28H] and TNFRSF18 [GITR]), and reduced NF-κB signaling (NFKB1 and RELB; Figure 4B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral NK cells showed downregulated stimulatory receptors (TMIGD2 [CD28H] and TNFRSF18 [GITR]).
source: Similar trends were observed for the peripheral NK cell population with peripherally reduced IFN response (MX1 and IFI44L), and proliferative genes (STMN1, HELLS, CENPF, PTTG1, and DNPH1), downregulated stimulatory receptors (TMIGD2 [CD28H] and TNFRSF18 [GITR]), and reduced NF-κB signaling (NFKB1 and RELB; Figure 4B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral NK cells showed reduced NF-κB signaling (NFKB1 and RELB).
source: Similar trends were observed for the peripheral NK cell population with peripherally reduced IFN response (MX1 and IFI44L), and proliferative genes (STMN1, HELLS, CENPF, PTTG1, and DNPH1), downregulated stimulatory receptors (TMIGD2 [CD28H] and TNFRSF18 [GITR]), and reduced NF-κB signaling (NFKB1 and RELB; Figure 4B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral NK cells showed upregulation of key genes associated with NK cell effector function (e.g. FCGR3A [CD16], FGFBP2, ITGB2, GZMH, and KIR2DS4).
source: Although, we observed upregulation of key genes associated with NK cell effector function in the periphery (e.g. FCGR3A [CD16], FGFBP2, ITGB2, GZMH, and KIR2DS4), increased expression of inhibitory receptors like LILRB1 and KLRG1, the latter especially in co-expression with chemokine receptor CX3CR1, identified the peripheral NK cells rather to be terminally differentiated with impaired cytotoxic capabilities (Sciumè et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Peripheral NK cells showed increased expression of inhibitory receptors LILRB1 and KLRG1.
source: Although, we observed upregulation of key genes associated with NK cell effector function in the periphery (e.g. FCGR3A [CD16], FGFBP2, ITGB2, GZMH, and KIR2DS4), increased expression of inhibitory receptors like LILRB1 and KLRG1, the latter especially in co-expression with chemokine receptor CX3CR1, identified the peripheral NK cells rather to be terminally differentiated with impaired cytotoxic capabilities (Sciumè et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: KLRG1 in co-expression with CX3CR1 identifies peripheral NK cells as terminally differentiated with impaired cytotoxic capabilities.
source: Although, we observed upregulation of key genes associated with NK cell effector function in the periphery (e.g. FCGR3A [CD16], FGFBP2, ITGB2, GZMH, and KIR2DS4), increased expression of inhibitory receptors like LILRB1 and KLRG1, the latter especially in co-expression with chemokine receptor CX3CR1, identified the peripheral NK cells rather to be terminally differentiated with impaired cytotoxic capabilities (Sciumè et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on gene expression patterns and cited literature.

claim: Peripheral NK cells showed abrogated cytokine activity profile with reduced expression of XCL1, XCL2, LTB, and CKLF.
source: This was in line with the observed abrogated cytokine activity profile in the peripheral NK cells with reduced expression of key factors like XCL1, XCL2, LTB, and CKLF.
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: There were large transcriptomic differences between PBMC and periphery CD8+ T cells with 1,417 differentially expressed genes (864 genes upregulated in the tumor periphery and 553 genes upregulated in PBMC).
source: Strikingly, there were large transcriptomic differences between PBMC and periphery CD8+ T cells (Figure 5A), with 1,417 differentially expressed genes (864 genes upregulated in the tumor periphery and 553 genes upregulated in PBMC; Figure 5B, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from differential expression analysis.

claim: CX3CR1 was one of the key genes upregulated in PBMC CD8+ T cells.
source: Interestingly, one of the key genes upregulated in PBMC CD8+ T cells was the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Flow cytometry confirmed an increased abundance of CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells in PBMC compared to almost absent CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells in tumor periphery.
source: Flow cytometry of an additional matched glioma grade 4 patient cohort confirmed an increased abundance of CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells in PBMC compared to almost absent CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells in tumor periphery (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry validation.

claim: CX3CR1 expression labelled a specific subpopulation among PBMC CD8+ T cells.
source: Unsupervised hierarchical sub-clustering of CD8+ T cells revealed that CX3CR1 expression labelled a specific subpopulation among PBMC CD8+ T cells (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from sub-clustering analysis.

claim: Expression of CX3CR1 was demonstrated to distinguish memory CD8+ T cells with cytotoxic effector function in healthy donors and different inflammation related conditions.
source: Recently, expression of CX3CR1 was demonstrated to distinguish memory CD8+ T cells with cytotoxic effector function in healthy donors and different inflammation related conditions (Böttcher et al., 2015; Gerlach et al., 2016; Yamauchi et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: A novel CX3CR1int subpopulation termed peripheral memory (Tpm) was identified.
source: Further characterization of classical central memory (Tcm) and effector memory (Tem) populations by varying surface expression levels of CX3CR1 identified a novel CX3CR1int subpopulation, termed peripheral memory (Tpm).
evidence: This is based on cited literature describing this population.

claim: Tpm cells underwent frequent homeostatic divisions, re-acquired CD62L, homed to lymph nodes, and predominantly surveyed peripheral tissues compared to Tcm and Tem.
source: Tpm cells underwent frequent homeostatic divisions, re-acquired CD62L, homed to lymph nodes, and predominantly surveyed peripheral tissues compared to Tcm and Tem (Gerlach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gerlach et al., 2016.

claim: Circulating CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells displayed a core signature of memory CD8+ T cells with effector function, comprising expression of LFA-1 (IGAL- ITGB2), TBX2 (Tbet), SELL (CD62L), GZMB (Granzyme B), and PRF1 (Perforin 1).
source: In our dataset, the circulating CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells indeed displayed a core signature of memory CD8+ T cells with effector function, comprising expression of LFA-1 (IGAL- ITGB2), TBX2 (Tbet), SELL (CD62L), GZMB (Granzyme B), and PRF1 (Perforin 1; Figure 5F), separating them from circulating CX3CR1- CD28high, IL7Rhigh and CD27high naïve CD8+ T cells (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis.

claim: Flow cytometric analysis confirmed Teff to be CX3CR1high, with negligible expression levels in the naïve CD8+ T cells, whereas the identified memory CD8+ T cells (Tem and Tpm) were CX3CR1int.
source: Flow cytometric analysis confirmed Teff to be CX3CR1high, with negligible expression levels in the naïve CD8+ T cells, whereas the identified memory CD8+ T cells (Tem and Tpm) were CX3CR1int (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Surface staining for CD45RA and CD45RO attributed a predominant CD45RO+ memory phenotype to the tumor infiltrating CD8+ T cells.
source: Surface staining for CD45RA and CD45RO, discriminating naïve/effector from memory T cells, attributed a predominant CD45RO+ memory phenotype to the tumor infiltrating CD8+ T cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: Tumor infiltrating CD8+ T cells showed key marker expression signature consistent with tissue-resident memory T cells (Trm).
source: Interrogation of the transcriptomic profile of these cells revealed a key marker expression signature consistent with tissue-resident memory T cells (Trm): Expression of cellular adhesion molecules (integrins) ITGA1 (CD49a) and ITGAE (CD103), tissue retention marker CD69, chemokine receptors implicated in tissue-homing CXCR3, CXCR6, and CCR5 (Urban et al., 2020) and transcription factors, ZNF683 (Hobit) and PRDM1 (Blimp1) as well as reduced expression of TBX21 (Tbet) and EOMES (Mackay et al., 2016), strongly suggested a Trm phenotype for these cells (Figure 6C and D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, with citations supporting the Trm characterization.

claim: Co-expression analysis using flow cytometry showed that CD69+ CD103- and CD69+ CD103+ cells are the dominant CD8+ T cell populations in the tumor periphery.
source: Co-expression analysis of paired PBMC and tumor periphery samples using flow cytometry showed that CD69+ CD103- and CD69+ CD103+ cells are the dominant CD8+ T cell populations in the tumor periphery (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis.

claim: CD8+ T cells in the tumor periphery showed increased expression of genes belonging to costimulatory pathways, including ICOS, TNFRSF4 (OX40) and TNFRSF9 (4-1BB).
source: Indeed, CD8+ T cells in the tumor periphery showed increased expression of genes belonging to costimulatory pathways, including ICOS, TNFRSF4 (OX40) and TNFRSF9 (4-1BB) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 6), albeit accompanied by high levels of inhibitory receptors PDCD1 (PD-1), LAG3, HAVCR2 (TIM-3), and CTLA4 (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: CD8+ T cells in the tumor periphery showed high levels of inhibitory receptors PDCD1 (PD-1), LAG3, HAVCR2 (TIM-3), and CTLA4.
source: Indeed, CD8+ T cells in the tumor periphery showed increased expression of genes belonging to costimulatory pathways, including ICOS, TNFRSF4 (OX40) and TNFRSF9 (4-1BB) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 6), albeit accompanied by high levels of inhibitory receptors PDCD1 (PD-1), LAG3, HAVCR2 (TIM-3), and CTLA4 (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: Expression of genes coding for cytotoxic molecules, including Granzyme B and Perforin 1 were decreased in the peripheral CD8+ T cells.
source: Moreover, expression of genes coding for cytotoxic molecules, including Granzyme B and Perforin 1 were decreased in the peripheral CD8+ T cells, suggesting a compromised killing capacity of these cells.
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: CD8+ T cells in the tumor periphery exhibited a transcription factor profile of exhausted T cells with high expression of NR4A1, MAF, and IRF4.
source: And lastly, CD8+ T cells in the tumor periphery exhibited a transcription factor profile of exhausted T cells with high expression of NR4A1, MAF, and IRF4 (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), which were implicated in T cell dysfunction and exhaustion (Ma et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, with citations supporting the exhaustion characterization.

claim: NR4A1, MAF, and IRF4 were implicated in T cell dysfunction and exhaustion.
source: And lastly, CD8+ T cells in the tumor periphery exhibited a transcription factor profile of exhausted T cells with high expression of NR4A1, MAF, and IRF4 (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), which were implicated in T cell dysfunction and exhaustion (Ma et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2019 and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: High upregulation of similar genes was observed in the comparison tumor periphery vs. PBMC for CD4+ T cells as for CD8+ T cells.
source: Noteworthy, we observed high upregulation of similar genes in the comparison tumor periphery vs. PBMC for CD4+ T cells as for CD8+ T cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis.

claim: NRA41-3 transcription factor family was identified as key mediator of T cell dysfunction.
source: These included transcription factor family NRA41-3, identified as key mediator of T cell dysfunction (Liu et al., 2019), Dual Specificity Protein Phosphatase 2/4 (DUSP2, DUSP4) described as negative regulators of mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase superfamily and associated with impaired T cell effector activity (Dan et al., 2020) and T cell senescence (Bignon et al., 2015), and transcription factor CREM which was implicated in IL-2 suppression (Maine et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: DUSP2 and DUSP4 are negative regulators of MAP kinase superfamily and associated with impaired T cell effector activity and T cell senescence.
source: These included transcription factor family NRA41-3, identified as key mediator of T cell dysfunction (Liu et al., 2019), Dual Specificity Protein Phosphatase 2/4 (DUSP2, DUSP4) described as negative regulators of mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase superfamily and associated with impaired T cell effector activity (Dan et al., 2020) and T cell senescence (Bignon et al., 2015), and transcription factor CREM which was implicated in IL-2 suppression (Maine et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dan et al., 2020 and Bignon et al., 2015.

claim: CREM was implicated in IL-2 suppression.
source: These included transcription factor family NRA41-3, identified as key mediator of T cell dysfunction (Liu et al., 2019), Dual Specificity Protein Phosphatase 2/4 (DUSP2, DUSP4) described as negative regulators of mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase superfamily and associated with impaired T cell effector activity (Dan et al., 2020) and T cell senescence (Bignon et al., 2015), and transcription factor CREM which was implicated in IL-2 suppression (Maine et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maine et al., 2016.

claim: These genes could potentially identify pan T cell dysfunction markers within the GBM iTME.
source: These genes could potentially identify pan T cell dysfunction markers within the GBM iTME (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement with citation support.

claim: SPP1 (Osteopontin) was revealed as a leading potential cell-cell interaction mediator between MG and lymphocytes in the tumor periphery.
source: We finally investigated cell-cell interactions based on ligand-receptor expression levels using the CellChat platform (Jin et al., 2021). Considering that MG and lymphocytes displayed an impaired activation signature in the tumor periphery, we focused our analysis on the tumor-peripheral crosstalk between these cells (Figure 7A). This revealed SPP1 (Osteopontin) as a leading potential cell-cell interaction mediator between MG and lymphocytes (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell interaction analysis using CellChat.

claim: MG SPP1-mediated signaling was among the most significant interactions when investigating cell-cell communication across all cell types and both sites.
source: MG SPP1-mediated signaling was as well among the most significant interactions, when investigating cell-cell communication across all cell types and both sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell interaction analysis.

claim: SPP1 is mainly expressed by MG rather than glioma cells.
source: Further, we found that SPP1 is mainly expressed by MG rather than glioma cells, contrary to previous reports (Wei et al., 2019; Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis, contrasting with cited literature.

claim: The predicted interactions of MG SPP1 with NK cells could be mediated via the integrin complex ITGA4-ITGB1 (CD49d-CD29).
source: MG SPP1 conveys different interactions, depending on the recipient cell binding receptor expression profile. The predicted interactions of MG SPP1 with NK cells could be mediated via the integrin complex ITGA4-ITGB1 (CD49d-CD29) (Figure 7A and C), whereas CD4+ and CD8+ T cells exhibited strong interactions with MG via SPP1/CD44 interaction (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is a prediction from cell-cell interaction analysis.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells exhibited strong interactions with MG via SPP1/CD44 interaction.
source: MG SPP1 conveys different interactions, depending on the recipient cell binding receptor expression profile. The predicted interactions of MG SPP1 with NK cells could be mediated via the integrin complex ITGA4-ITGB1 (CD49d-CD29) (Figure 7A and C), whereas CD4+ and CD8+ T cells exhibited strong interactions with MG via SPP1/CD44 interaction (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell interaction analysis.

claim: The SPP1/CD44 axis was recently described to suppress T cell activation and proliferation.
source: The SPP1/CD44 axis was recently described to suppress T cell activation and proliferation (Klement et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Klement et al., 2018.

claim: The identified MG SPP1-mediated interactions might represent potential targets to modulate MG-lymphocyte crosstalk in the tumor periphery.
source: The identified MG SPP1-mediated interactions might represent potential targets to modulate MG-lymphocyte crosstalk in the tumor periphery.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic implications.

claim: Previous studies focused on the description of the TME of grade 4 glioma primarily at neoplastic cells rather than the immune compartment.
source: Previous studies focused on the description of the TME of grade 4 glioma, which also considered regional differences, yet they focused primarily at neoplastic cells rather than the immune compartment (Darmanis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about previous literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Two studies reported differences in the iTME composition between IDH1wt and IDH1mut glioma.
source: Interestingly, the two latter ones reported differences in the iTME composition between IDH1wt and IDH1mut glioma.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from previous studies.

claim: A similar MG subpopulation expressing a comparable gene signature to MG_1 was recently described to be enriched in Alzheimer's disease patients.
source: A similar MG subpopulation expressing a comparable gene signature was recently described to be enriched in Alzheimer's disease patients (Olah et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Olah et al., 2020.

claim: Induction of an IFN response state was described as a consequence of T cell receptor-mediated IFN-γ production, likely serving as an autocrine response and inducing the proliferative program.
source: Induction of an IFN response state was described as a consequence of T cell receptor-mediated IFN-γ production, likely serving as an autocrine response and inducing the proliferative program (Szabo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Szabo et al., 2019.

claim: Treatment with anti-CD47, anti-PD1, or their combination induced an IFN-γ response only in the tumor center, but not periphery in GBM explants cultured in perfusion bioreactors.
source: Recently, we showed that the response to immunotherapy in GBM is indeed region dependent. For this, we cultured GBM explants in perfusion bioreactors and treated with anti-CD47, anti-PD1, or their combination which induced an IFN-γ response only in the tumor center, but not periphery (Shekarian et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shekarian et al., 2022.

claim: Adoptive transfer studies of CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells in a melanoma mouse model significantly suppressed tumor growth.
source: Recently, adoptive transfer studies of CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells in a melanoma mouse model significantly suppressed tumor growth (Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2018.

claim: Increased frequencies of CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells were found in non-small cell lung and melanoma patients who responded to anti-PD-1 therapy.
source: Others identified increased frequencies of CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells in non-small cell lung and melanoma patients who responded to anti-PD-1 therapy, where these cells exhibited migratory capabilities into the tumor site followed by potent tumor rejection (Yamauchi et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamauchi et al., 2021 and Yan et al., 2018.

claim: T cell CX3CR1 expression was proposed as a predictor of response to ICI therapy.
source: Thus, the authors proposed T cell CX3CR1 expression as a predictor of response to ICI therapy.
evidence: This is a statement about a proposal from cited literature.

claim: The absence of CX3CR1+ effector CD8+ T cells in the glioma TME could serve as an additional explanation for the disappointing outcome of clinical trials using ICI in glioma patients.
source: Even though CX3CR1+ CD8+ T cells might not be specific to GBM, as they are found in healthy donor and different inflammation related conditions (Böttcher et al., 2015; Gerlach et al., 2016; Yamauchi et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2018), the absence of these effector and potentially ICI therapy responsive CD8+ T cells in the glioma TME could serve as an additional explanation for the disappointing outcome of clinical trials using ICI in glioma patients.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: The observed Trm exhaustion phenotype of the glioma residing CD8+ T cells was recently reported for tumor-infiltrating PD-1high CD8+ T cells in hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: The observed Trm exhaustion phenotype of the glioma residing CD8+ T cells was recently reported as well for tumor-infiltrating PD-1high CD8+ T cells in hepatocellular carcinoma (Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2019.

claim: A consistent brain-resident CD8+ T cell population was reported in an autopsy cohort of patients with neurological disorders and patients with no known brain disease.
source: Particularly in the light of a recent study by Smolders and colleagues who reported a consistent brain-resident CD8+ T cell population in a miscellaneous autopsy cohort of patients with neurological disorders excluding brain malignancies (Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, dementia, depression, multiple sclerosis), as well as patients with no known brain disease.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from Smolders and colleagues.

claim: Brain-resident CD8+ T cells displayed a remarkably consistent Trm phenotype.
source: These brain-resident CD8+ T cells displayed a remarkably consistent Trm phenotype (Smolders et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smolders et al., 2018.

claim: Brain CD8+ Trm cells showed high expression of inhibitory receptors CTLA-4 and PD-1.
source: The authors further showed high expression of inhibitory receptors CTLA-4 and PD-1 on the brain-resident CD8+ Trm cells, which is in line with the core phenotypic signature of Trm cells from other tissues (Kumar et al., 2017; Mackay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from cited literature.

claim: Brain CD8+ Trm cells showed a preserved inflammatory potential with substantial production of IFN-γ and TNF-α upon ex vivo stimulation.
source: Yet, the brain CD8+ Trm cells showed a preserved inflammatory potential with substantial production of IFN-γ and TNF-α upon ex vivo stimulation.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from cited literature.

claim: Inhibitory receptors like PD-1 and CTLA-4 on brain CD8+ Trm cells may support CNS homeostasis by preventing uncontrolled T cell reactivity.
source: Therefore, inhibitory receptors like PD-1 and CTLA-4 on brain CD8+ Trm cells may support CNS homeostasis by preventing uncontrolled T cell reactivity, and the availability of the receptor ligands may determine their inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: The tumor setting leads to disruption of the equilibrium with upregulation of inhibitory ligands like PD-L1 on glioma cells and CD86 on GAMs, leading to the dysfunctional state seen in the glioma-residing CD8+ Trm cells.
source: While this may represent a well-balanced equilibrium under healthy conditions, the tumor setting leads to its disruption with upregulation of inhibitory ligands like PD-L1 on glioma cells and CD86 on GAMs, leading to the dysfunctional state seen in the glioma-residing CD8+ Trm cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings and biological knowledge.

claim: Peripheral infections generate antigen-specific CD8+ Trm cells in the brain, mediating protection against CNS infections.
source: Another study comprehensively showed, that peripheral infections generate antigen-specific CD8+ Trm cells in the brain, mediating protection against CNS infections (Urban et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Urban et al., 2020.

claim: SPP1 was found to be differentially expressed in aging-microglia and associated with a doubling of the abundance of SPP1+ GAMs in GBM samples compared to MG from age-matched controls.
source: In a comprehensive approach where transcriptional states of human MG were mapped during aging and disease, SPP1 was found to be differentially expressed in aging-microglia. This was associated to a doubling of the abundance of SPP1+ GAMs in GBM samples compared to MG from age-matched controls (Sankowski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sankowski et al., 2019.

claim: Myeloid-derived osteopontin (encoded by SPP1) was shown to trigger a chronic activation of NFAT2 in tumor-reactive CD8+ T cells, leading to T cell dysfunction and exhaustion in an experimental mouse model of GBM.
source: More recently, myeloid-derived osteopontin (encoded by SPP1) was shown to trigger a chronic activation of NFAT2 in tumor-reactive CD8+ T cells, leading to T cell dysfunction and exhaustion in an experimental mouse model of GBM (Kilian et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kilian et al., 2023.
